children: As AI absorbs routine tasks and fresher hiring slows, Sayantani Dutta argues that organisations risk weakening the early-career experiences that build judgement and future leaders
As AI absorbs entry-level work, organisations may be dismantling the very layer where judgment, expertise, and future leaders are formed.

India recorded 3.5 lakh AI-related job openings in a single quarter, according to a June 2026 Quess Corp report. Nearly half require three to five years of hands-on experience, even as fresher hiring continues to decline. Only 2.57 lakh professionals are currently engaged in advanced AI domains, where 70 percent of demand now sits.
The mismatch is not merely one of supply. It reflects a shrinking pool of professionals gaining the early-career experience required to grow into these roles.

The data does not simply describe a talent shortage. It describes a development gap—one that organisations may be widening as they reduce junior hiring while relying increasingly on experienced talent.
The Leaders of 2030 Are Not Being Formed

EY's AIdea of India 2026 report documents this shift in precise terms. In India's technology services sector, many firms have already consolidated 20–25 percent of entry-level roles through AI and automation. One leading IT services firm reduced entry-level hiring by nearly 30 percent while increasing mid-career hiring by 20 percent. Fresher hiring, the report notes, is slowing "not due to lack of business, but because entry-level work is evaporating as AI fills the gap."
The report raises a question that deserves far more strategic attention: "If AI handles all the grunt work, who is building judgment?"

It is being treated as a tension to manage, but it should be treated as a strategic workforce risk. Efficiency can eliminate tasks far faster than organisations can rebuild the capabilities those tasks once created.
What Entry-Level Work Was Actually Doing

The conventional framing of entry-level roles is about task execution: the routine, the administrative, the repeatable. AI absorbing these tasks looks like straightforward efficiency. Why staff a junior to do what a tool can do in minutes?
The tasks were never the point. The development was.

Professional judgment is not built solely through training programmes or credentials. It is built through friction: through badly written briefs, clients who change their minds, conflicting stakeholder expectations, and decisions made under uncertainty, through being wrong, adjusting, and becoming less wrong the next time.

This concern also aligns with a broader global trend. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 finds that employers expect nearly 40 percent of workers' core skills to change by 2030. Yet it leaves open a harder question: where will those capabilities be developed if the entry-level experiences that once built judgment are disappearing?

That formation cannot be delegated to a tool. When organisations compress or eliminate these early developmental experiences, they risk removing many of the conditions through which future leaders have traditionally become capable.

The mid-career professionals hired today are likely to become the senior leaders of 2030 and 2031. What is being determined right now, through reduced fresher intake and shrinking entry-level opportunities, is who fills leadership roles beyond that.

Many professionals entering organisations today may begin their careers in environments where AI resolves the low-level problems before those problems have a chance to teach them anything. They may become highly productive with AI tools while having fewer opportunities to develop judgment through repeated exposure to ambiguity, trade-offs and failure.
This is not simply a talent acquisition issue. It is a talent development issue, and most organisations are not yet modelling it.
The Compounding Problem

The challenge begins well before organisations make hiring decisions. NASSCOM and Aspiring Minds assessments consistently find that only 43–45 percent of Indian graduates are immediately employable for meaningful roles.

Historically, organisations relied on structured early-career experiences to bridge this readiness gap. As AI compresses entry-level work, one of the industry's most important mechanisms for converting potential into capability is also shrinking.
At the same time, the instruments used to identify high-potential talent are themselves evolving.
Candidates increasingly optimise applications using AI. Employers increasingly screen applications using AI.
This does not necessarily produce better matching. It may instead create more sophisticated noise, making it harder to distinguish genuine capability from a well-optimised profile.
We have made the filter more sophisticated while making the signal weaker.

Capability is also emerging through increasingly diverse pathways, including AI-enabled self-learning and talent development outside traditional metro ecosystems. This does not simplify identification but makes it more consequential.

There is, of course, a counterargument: that AI removes repetitive work, letting young professionals contribute to higher-value activities far earlier. That opportunity is real, but only if organisations deliberately redesign developmental experiences rather than eliminating the work that once created them.
What This Calls For

The answer is not to preserve entry-level roles exactly as they existed, nor is it to slow AI adoption. The efficiency gains are real. The question is what organisations choose to protect while redesigning work. Entry-level roles should no longer be viewed primarily as cost centres. They are leadership pipeline investments.
The question is not what a junior employee can produce today.
It is what that individual will be capable of producing five years from now, and whether your organisation will be the one that develops that capability.

Alongside this, capability-based identification provides a more durable basis for selection than credentials or AI-optimised applications. This means evaluating how someone reasons through unfamiliar problems, responds to ambiguity, and learns under pressure.

Equally important, organisations may need to redesign entry-level roles around supervised judgment rather than routine execution. If AI produces the first draft, the developmental value lies in teaching young professionals how to question it, improve it, and ultimately take accountability for the final decision.
These are not new ideas, but ideas whose urgency has finally become impossible to ignore.
The Talent Creation Imperative

For most of the last century, leadership pipelines were treated primarily as talent acquisition challenges. Identify the right people, hire them, and develop them. What is becoming increasingly clear is that hiring talent and creating talent are no longer the same challenge. The defining talent challenge of the coming decade may not be talent acquisition, but talent creation.
The professionals who will lead organisations tomorrow are not waiting somewhere in the market to be discovered.
They are being formed—or not being formed—today, inside organisations exactly like yours.

The organisations that recognise this earliest will build a leadership advantage that no hiring budget can replicate. Those that do not, may spend the next decade searching for experienced leaders in an increasingly constrained market, wondering why leadership has become so difficult to hire despite investing heavily in recruitment.
Sayantani Dutta
Guest Author Chief Human Resource Officer, AdGlobal360
